Abstract
Web technologies are constantly evolving. JavaScript, CSS, and HTML are getting new
versions and web browsers provide more APIs for web developers. But users are visiting
these web pages on a wide variety of web browsers, that have varying levels of support
for these latest features. Additionally, users are not updating their browsers to the latest
versions immediately. The web page should still work for most users. On the other hand,
these new features make developing web pages and applications easier and allow new
possibilities for what pages and applications can do. So, the question becomes how to
serve a functioning web page to all users and still allow the usage of the newest language
features in those pages.
One solution is to use a transpiler. A transpiler is a tool for converting source code from
one language to another. In web development, it is used to convert the latest language
version to an older version, so that it is supported in older browser versions. Another
complementary solution is polyfills. A polyfill is a JavaScript library that can add missing
APIs to browsers, so that code relying on these APIs will work.
This thesis focuses on improving the support of older browsers and the performance of
web browsers on the Iltalehti news website. Iltalehti already uses transpilers and polyfills
to support older browsers. This thesis will focus first on how to form a list of browser
versions that should be supported from website access analytics and updating the current
list to this new list. Second, how much transpilation target change affects file sizes and
thus website performance. And lastly, how automated testing can be used to ensure that
website is actually working in all these browser versions.

Keywords transpiler, polyfill, web application, website, web development

Tiivistelmä
Verkkoteknologiat kehittyvät jatkuvasti. JavaScript, CSS ja HTML saavat uusia versioita ja verkkoselaimet tarjoavat yhä uusia rajapintoja sivustojen kehittäjille. Mutta
käyttäjät vierailevat sivustoilla eri selaimilla, joista jokaisella on erilainen tuki näille
uusille ominaisuuksille. Lisäksi käyttäjät eivät päivitä selaimiaan heti uusimpaan versioon. Toisaalta nämä uudet ominaisuudet tekevät sivustojen kehittämisestä helpompaa
ja tarjoavat uusia mahdollisuuksia sivustojen ja verkkosovellusten toimintaan. Haasteena
on kuinka samaan aikaan tarjotaan kaikille käyttäjille toimiva sivusto sekä mahdollistetaan näiden uusien ominaisuuksien käyttö sivustolla.
Yksi ratkaisu tähän on kääntäjä, joka kääntää yhden ohjelmointikielen lähdekoodia
toisen ohjelmointikielen lähdekoodiksi. Verkkosivujen kehittämisessä tämäntyyppistä
kääntäjää käytetään kääntämään ohjelmointikielen uusimman version mukaista lähdekoodia vanhempaan versioon, jotta se toimisi myös vanhemmissa selaimissa. Tämän
lisäksi käytetään JavaScript-kirjastoja, jotka lisäävät vanhempiin selaimiin puuttuvia
rajapintoja.
Tämä diplomityö keskittyy parantamaan tukea vanhoille selaimille ja parantamaan
suorituskykyä Iltalehden uutisverkkosivustolla. Iltalehdessä käytetään jo mainittuja
tapoja vanhojen selaiminen tukemiseksi. Ensiksi koostetaan lista selaimien versioista
ja käyttäjämääristä Iltalehdessä kävijämittauksen perusteella. Seuraavaksi tämän listan perusteella päivitetään tuettujen selaimien listaa Iltalehdessä ja tutkitaan kuinka
paljon tämä vaikuttaa sivuston muodostavien tiedostojen kokoon ja tätä myötä suorituskykyyn. Viimeiseksi tutkitaan kuinka Iltalehden selaintuen toimivuutta voidaan varmistaa
automaatiotestauksen avulla.

Avainsanat transpiler, polyfill, verkkosovellus, verkkosivusto, verkkokehitys

1. Introduction

The web platform is constantly evolving. JavaScript, CSS, and HTML are
getting new versions and web browsers provide more APIs for web pages.
But users are visiting these web pages on a wide variety of web browsers,
that have varying levels of support for the latest features. Additionally,
users are not updating their browsers to the latest versions immediately.
The web page should still work for all users. Oppositely these new features
make developing web pages and applications easier and allow new possibilities for what pages and applications can do. So, the question becomes
how to serve a functioning web page to all users and still use the newest
language features in those pages.
One solution is to use a transpiler. Transpiler is a tool for converting
source code from one language to another. In web development, it is used
to convert the latest language version to an older version, so that it is
supported in older browser versions. Another complementary solution is
polyfills. A polyfill is a JavaScript library that can add missing APIs to
browsers, so that code relying on these APIs will work.
This thesis is a case study about improving support of older browsers and
the performance of web browsers on the Iltalehti news website. Iltalehti
already uses transpilers and polyfills to support older browsers. This thesis
will focus first on how to form a list of browser versions that should be
supported from site access analytics and updating the current list to this
new list. Second, how much transpilation target change affects file sizes
and thus site performance. And lastly, if end-to-end testing can be used to
ensure that site is actually working in all these browser versions.

7

Introduction

1.1

Objectives

The objective of this thesis is to improve the transpilation setup of the
Iltalehti website build process. This is split into three different cases.
The first case is supporting more relevant browser versions by adjusting, which browser versions are targeted in transpilation. More relevant
meaning browser versions that are the most used on the Iltalehti website.
The second case is smaller file sizes by targeting just browsers that
are used. Smaller file sizes will usually yield better performance for the
website.
Web page performance metrics can be measured directly, which should
be better with smaller file sizes, but for simplicity, the focus will be on
just file sizes. The actual performance of the page can also change when
targeted browsers for transpilation change as produced code changes and
performs differently.
The last is ensuring that the website really works for all these browsers
by testing it on a variety of browsers. An already existing automated
integration test suite is used as a base and it is converted to run on
multiple browsers.
In the process of making these improvements, answers to the following
research questions are searched:

• RQ1: What is the coverage of the current transpilation setup in browsers
used to visit the Iltalehti website and can a higher coverage percentage
be achieved?

• RQ2: How much does adjusting targeted browsers affect file sizes?

• RQ3: Can browser support be tested with end-to-end tests and what are
the advantages and disadvantages of testing on multiple browsers?

1.2

Structure of the Thesis

The thesis is separated into five main chapters, and the introductory
chapter.
The second chapter explains what are transpilation and polyfills and how
they are used in web development.

8

Introduction

The third chapter introduces the Iltalehti news website and how transpilation and polyfills are used on the code-base of the website.
The fourth chapter goes through the implementation of the changes to
the Iltalehti website.
The fifth chapter discusses the results of the changes made to the Iltalehti
website. It also discusses alternatives to transpilation in web development.
The sixth chapter concludes the thesis.

9

2. Background

This chapter describes what is transpilation and why it is used in web
development. The first two sections will describe what is a transpiler and
a polyfill. Sections 2.3, 2.4, and 2.5 will give examples of transpilers used
in web development.
Then Section 2.8 will explain what is a Web Application and a few terms
closely related to it.
Sections 2.7, 2.8, and 2.9 will go through the web languages (JavaScript,
CSS, and HTML) and explain what is the process of them gaining new
features. It will also look what are the methods for supporting these new
features in older browsers.
Sections 2.10 and 2.11 focus on web browsers: how transpilation is
supported in them with source maps and what kind of data is available
about support for different features in web browsers.

2.1

Transpiler

A transpiler is a tool for converting source code written in a high-level language (source language) to another high-level language (target language).
Another name for a transpiler is a source-to-source compiler. Transpiler is
similar to a compiler, that converts source code from a high-level language
to a lower-level language, the difference is in the output language. For
example source code written in C language is usually compiled to assembly
code to be executed. [38]
Transpiler generates source code as output, as a human could have authored, but the output is usually meant to be executed and so it fills a
similar role as a compiler as a step between source code and the actual
executed program. There are multiple use cases for transpiler, two notable
examples being the following: first is utilizing existing language’s compiler

10

Background

for generating bytecode or assembly, as authoring a compiler requires more
effort and it can be easier to just use an existing compiler. Especially, an optimizing compiler is a time-consuming and complicated project to develop,
and this allows reusing that work [30]. Another reason is compatibility
when targeting platforms that use a high-level language as a method of
executing code. Such as web browsers that are not updated to the latest
JavaScript standards. [38]
Listing 1 is an example of source and output when transpiling JavaScript
to JavaScript and replacing a new JavaScript feature optional chaining
operator (.?) so that following will work even on browsers that do not
support this feature.
// Original source code:
if (thing?.a === 2) {
// do something
}
// -----------------------------------------------------------------------// Transpiled source code:
if ((thing === null || thing === void 0 ? void 0 : thing.a) === 2) {
// do something
}

Listing 1. Example of transpilation output produced by Babel [3] when using a JavaScript
feature called optional chaining operator .?. In the output, the syntax is
replaced with other language constructs that will produce identical results.

2.2

Polyfill

Polyfill is a newer term that is used in web development to refer to a library
that implements a missing feature in web browsers. Polyfills are used to
add newer features to older browsers and to add new not yet standardized
features to current browsers. Polyfills are usually written in JavaScript,
but some exist that are based on other technologies (e.g., there exists a
polyfill for HTML Canvas element on Microsoft Internet Explorer 7 using
a Silverlight plugin [34]). Polyfills can provide missing or fix incomplete
browser APIs (e.g., the Fetch API [43]) that are not part of JavaScript
language or they can provide JavaScript language features that are not
based on new language syntax. Listing 2 gives an example of polyfill for
Array.prototype.includes method, which is part of JavaScript language.
[34]
Polyfilling (the act of providing a polyfill) is usually needed with transpiling newer versions of JavaScript for standard library changes and

11

Background

Array.prototype.includes = function(value) {
return this.indexOf(value) !== -1;
};
// Now these work:
[1, 2, 3].includes(2); // -> true
[1, 2, 3].includes(4); // -> false

Listing 2. An example polyfill of JavaScripts Array.prototype.includes method for environments that support Array.prototype.indexOf, but not includes. Note that this is
a simplified example and does not match the specification.

some transpiled language features need a runtime library to provide some
missing functionality. [34]
JavaScript’s ability to dynamically redefine nearly everything, which is
usually seen as a negative feature, is what makes polyfills possible. [15]
As demonstrated in the Listing 2, one can add a method for Array, a part of
the standard library and it will be conveniently available in all instances
of Array.

2.3

Babel

Babel is a JavaScript transpiler that can be used to transform future
JavaScript to an older version. This can be used to support web browsers
that do not yet support the latest features and trying out newer not yet standardized features. Babel is modular software: the transpilation pipeline
is split into multiple modules and its function can be customized with
different plugins. With plugins, Babel can do other transformations than
just handling JavaScript code, e.g. JSX syntax in JavaScript files, which is
commonly used with React library, can be parsed with its own plugin. [4]
Babel provides both the CLI program and JavaScript API for instructing
it. It also provides integration to different JavaScript build tools. Iltalehti
code base uses Webpack as a build tool and with it Webpack integration of
Babel. [4]
The main stages of the transpilation process in Babel are parsing, transforming, and generating. In the parsing stage, source code goes through
first lexical analysis and then syntactic analysis. Lexing will convert a
source code string to a stream of tokens. The syntactic analysis will convert
these tokens to Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). [4]
To explain this parsing process, we can look at a simple example piece of
code through these steps. Listing 3 shows a simple example source code
input that will be processed by Babel.

12

Background

1 + x;

Listing 3. Example JavaScript source code as input to Babel.
[
{
"type": { "label": "num", ... },
"value": 1,
"start": 0,
"end": 1,
"loc": { ... }
},
{
"type": { "label": "+/-", ... },
"value": "+",
"start": 2,
"end": 3,
"loc": { ... }
},
{

"value": "x",
"start": 4,
"end": 5,

{

},
{

"start": 6,
"end": 6,
"loc": { ... }
}
]

Listing 4. Stream of tokens from Babel after lexical analysis of 1 + x;.

The first lexical analysis step produces a list of tokens from the source
code. The data structure is just a flat list of language syntax pieces as can
be seen in Listing 4. [4]
Next, Listing 5 shows AST produced from these tokens. It is a tree
structure and the format is designed to be easy to work within the transformation step. [4]
Transform is a stage that contains the main work of Babel, and here AST
nodes are updated, moved, added, or removed. Here plugins will handle

transforming code to a format that older browsers can support. [4]

2.4

PostCSS

PostCSS is a CSS transpiler that can be customized with plugins. The
architecture of PostCSS is very similar to Babel that is used for JavaScript.
The actual browser support modifications are done with Autoprefixer,
which is a plugin for PostCSS. Autoprefixer adds vendor prefixes to CSS.
[2]
PostCSS compilation process consists of first parsing CSS files to AST,
this is split to lexing and parsing steps, then processor step where plugins
are run and lastly stringification, where output CSS is produced. Figure 1
shows these steps. [32]

14

Background

Figure 1. PostCSS workflow [32]

2.5

Browserslist

Different front-end tools need a list of targeted browser versions to perform
transpilation and other tasks related to that. Browserslist is a tool that
allows creating queries that are transformed to a list of targeted browsers
to multiple tools. [8]
Queries can contain references to global usage statistics that are delivered with the Browserslist tool, so the developer can specify that he
wants to support x% of users. It can contain also absolute browser name
and version requirements, or relative version requirements (such as last
2 versions. Listing 6 shows an example query that contains all of these
requirements.
last 2 version
> 1%
IE 11

Listing 6. An example query.

Browserslist query can also contain references to your own statistics
(provided with an additional file), so you can target specifically your users
as seen in the Listing 7).

15

Background

> 2% in my stats

Listing 7. Browserslists allows using custom statistics collected from users in your website.

2.6

Web Application

Web application term is used to describe websites with application-like
features, for example, webmail, which are not just static web pages but
contain interactive elements. This term is discussed here because typically
a web application has more functionality in it, and therefore has more
source code in them. This in turn means that techniques described here
(transpilation and polyfills) are more relevant as it makes writing this
larger amount of code easier by using the latest features and not worrying
so much about browser support. Web applications also typically use more
browser APIs to provide more features, so their availability is important.
[41]

2.6.1

Single Page Application

A Single Page Application (SPA) is a web application that fetches only
one HTML page from the server when a user first navigates to it and all
rendering is done with JavaScript on the web browser. On page change
client code modifies page URL and fetches new data for the new page and
updates the UI with JavaScript. [13]

2.6.2

Server-Side Rendering

Server-Side Rendering (SSR) is a technique used by SPAs to speed up
the rendering of the first page when a user first comes to the website.
Later page changes are fast in SPA, but the first page will require the
initialization of the whole application, which worsens the user experience
on the first page load. Without SSR the first HTML page from the server
would only contain URLs for scripts and styles, but no actual page content
in HTML. Then, JavaScript would execute and fetch the necessary data
and transform it to content on the page. With SSR this first fetching
and page render is done already on the server and the generated page is
returned to the client. The client application must then be able to start
from this point, which is called hydration. SSR is typically achieved with a
NodeJS server as it can run JavaScript code on the server-side. [20]

16

Background

2.7

JavaScript

JavaScript is a programming language. It is mainly used to add functionality to web pages, as web browsers support JavaScript natively. JavaScript
is originally designed for just this purpose, but today JavaScript can additionally be run outside web browsers with NodeJS. The standardized
version of JavaScript is called EcmaScript, because of trademark reasons
relating to its name. [15]

2.7.1

History

There have been multiple versions of JavaScript, from version 1 released
in 1995 to the latest ES 2021 version from the current year. Up to version
5, versions were identified with an increasing number. [35]
Starting from version 6, ECMAScript has had yearly releases and versioning has changed from a rolling number to a year when the version was
released. So, ECMAScript 6 is ECMAScript 2015. Sometimes a shortened
form ES 2015 is used. The latest version as of writing is ES 2021. [35]
Web browsers provide the best support for JavaScript as a language to
develop web pages and applications with. There are other options in web
browsers like WebAssembly, but it is a relatively young technology and has
some limitations compared to JavaScript. [9] Some other options are Java
and ActionScript (Flash applets), but they require the use of additional
browser extensions and their popularity is decreasing and some browsers
disallow these extensions completely. [1] [21]

2.7.2

Standardization and Development

JavaScript is specified by the TC39 committee in ECMA. Its development
is based on proposals that are made to the committee. Proposals have
four stages that they move through before being included in the standard.
Accepting a proposal to the standard requires that it has two independent
implementations and an earlier stage of the proposal should have a polyfill
for proposals feature if possible. This is required so that proposals have
actual working code and it ensures that they can be implemented before
being included in the standard. [35]
New experimental JavaScript features can be supported in browsers with
just polyfills, for features not having new syntax in the language, or with
transpilation if they contain new syntax. Sometimes both are needed.

17

Background

In addition to the JavaScript programming language, there are different
browser APIs that can be used from JavaScript. These can sometimes be
supported with polyfills, but some new features can not be supported in any
way in unsupported browsers. For example, bringing device orientation API
support needs the browser to supply the actual data for device orientation.
Using new JavaScript features in browsers that do not support them
most often leads to exceptions or other errors. In HTML and CSS, newer
features are usually designed so that they are backward compatible and
will not cause the page to be completely unusable. But with JavaScript this
can happen, so developers need to be more careful especially in websites
that rely heavily on JavaScript. This also means that transpilation and
polyfills are more important for JavaScript.

2.8

CSS

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is a language for defining styles (font, color,
and layout) for web pages.

2.8.1

History

CSS has existed nearly as long as web browsers have, the first specification
of CSS is CSS level 1 published in 1996 [14]. The first two versions of CSS
were released as single specifications. A revision to level 2, level 2.1 saw
many status changes lasting many years as it had to be revised multiple
times. After that, there has not been a single specification, and instead,
CSS 3 consists of multiple small specifications called "modules", that each
have independent status and are implemented in browsers module by
module. [39]

2.8.2

Standardization and Development

CSS is standardized by W3C in the CSS working group. The latest stable
version of CSS is CSS Snapshot 2020, which describes what modules are
stable as of 2020 [40]. Snapshots are not meant for developers writing
CSS, but for browser vendors as a guide to what features to implement
in browsers. Developers need to check support status separately for each
module. CSS is not versioned in yearly versions as EcmaScript is, but
instead, it evolves by gaining single modules to the language. Each module
brings only a single or a few features at a time. [39]

18

Background

New experimental features have been added with vendor prefixes to
browsers so that they can be tried out before they are released. When a
feature has been released officially as non-prefixed to the latest browsers,
these prefixed rules are used by web developers to add support to older
browsers into their pages. Sometimes these experimental features are used
on websites even before they have non-prefixed versions in any browser.
Different browser versions can be supported by specifying the same CSS
rules with different prefixes: for example, WebKit-based browsers (such as
Chrome and Safari) use a prefix of -webkit-. [29]
Example usage of prefixes in CSS files can be seen in Listing 8.
-webkit-border-radius: 8px;
-moz-border-radius: 8px;
-o-border-radius: 8px;
-ms-border-radius: 8px;
border-radius: 8px;

Listing 8. Example usage of CSS property border-radius with prefixes for different
browsers.

But this is planned to change, as browser vendors are working to stop
using vendor prefixes for experimental features. This is done because these
vendor prefixes were never meant to be used on production websites and
instead just to test out new features. [29]
Some CSS features can be polyfilled with JavaScript polyfills if there
exists no prefixed rule to add support. For example, CSS feature position:
sticky that makes element follow users scrolling can be polyfilled with a
JavaScript polyfill [23]. Browsers support for different CSS features can be
queried with @supports media rule, it can be used to define two different
styles, one using a modern CSS feature and one fallback style. [27]

2.9

HTML

HTML5 (i.e., the latest version of HTML) is standardized by both W3C
and WHATWG. The term HTML5 is sometimes used to describe modern
web technologies, not just as a version for HTML files. When HTML5 was
created it tried to specify existing parsing quirks, for example, unclosed
<p> tags, that were created to parse websites even when the website author
had made some mistakes. Parsers skipping over undetected content is also
a feature that is specified and it allows introducing new elements and tags
to HTML format without breaking existing implementations. [44]

19

Background

<img src="image.jpg" loading="lazy">

Listing 9. For example attribute loading="lazy" is a newer feature in HTML. Unsupported
browsers will ignore this attribute when parsing HTML and load images eagerly.
Others will defer the loading of the image until the user scrolls so that the
image is visible. [44]

Because HTML parsing is liberal, new features can be added to it easily,
as Listing 9 demonstrates.
Polyfills are used to add support for newer features in nonsupporting
browsers. These are usually JavaScript scripts. For example, betterdateinput-polyfill [19] can be used to polyfill date picker to <input type="date" />
elements. Polyfill uses JavaScript to search HTML document for these
elements and provide a fallback for the date picker, as not all browsers
support this feature.

2.10

Source Map

One concern when developing web pages, that use generated code from
transpiler, is how it affects debugging. Having only the generated code
available in debugging tools in a web browser complicates debugging, as
users need to mentally map source code locations to locations in generated
code with syntax differences in these files. Additionally, web page source
code might be minified to reduce file sizes (whitespace removed, variable
and function names shortened, and so on), which makes this task even
harder. [22]
Source Maps are a feature in web browsers that provide a mapping from
generated code to source code. This feature consists of a file format for
source map files and a comment format with linking URLs for generated
files. Source map files have conventionally the same name as the target file
with an additional extension of .map (but it is not required). The linking
comment (cf. Listing 10) is meant to be placed at the end of the generated
source code file and it contains a URL for the corresponding source map
file (cf. Listing 11). Source maps are specified in Source Map Revision 3
Proposal [24]. [22]
//# sourceMappingURL=main.js.map

Listing 10. Example of sourceMappingURL comment for a file named main.js. It is added
at the end of main.js.

When source maps are available browser can show stack traces from
original files in the console, for example, when an exception is thrown and

20

Background

{
"version": 3,
"file": "main.js",
"sourceRoot": "",
"sources": ["foo.js", "bar.js"],
"names": ["src", "maps", "are", "fun"],
"mappings": "A,AAAB;;ABCDE;"
}

Listing 11. Example of source mapping file for main.js. This is a separate file from
main.js.

a debugger can step through original source code. Source maps work both
for JavaScript and CSS files. [22]
Additionally, Source Maps are not just for JavaScript and CSS, but other
languages can use them too if they transpile to JavaScript or CSS. [22]
Sometimes source maps are concealed from end-users, as they can be
used to reveal the actual source code for the page. Hiding them will
obfuscate the code and make revealing vulnerabilities in the code harder.
[31]

2.11

Browser Support

For transpilation to function we need to establish some minimum level
of supported language features so that we know which features need
transpilation which can be left as is. One could generate this information
by testing all features in different web browser versions and by reading
release notes from web browsers where new features are announced.
Fortunately, this data is already available from multiple sources. One of
them is the canisuse.com website, which provides support tables for many
JavaScript, CSS, and HTML features. A developer can search features by
name and manually check how well it is supported. Additionally, the data
behind tables are also available in a machine-readable format. Browser
support tables in canisuse.com look like in Figure 2. canisuse.com uses a
test suite to generate some of the support data, in addition to manually
collecting this data by volunteers. [10]
Another source is MDN articles about web technologies. Most articles
about different JavaScript APIs and CSS features contain browser compatibility tables at the end of the page (as seen in Figure 3) [28]. This data is
collected and curated in @mdn/browser-compat-data repository on GitHub.
[26]

21

Background

Figure 2. browser support table from caniuse.com

Figure 3. Example of browser support data from MDN page of Array.prototype.includes()

ECMAScript compatibility tables provide more fine-grained support information about different JavaScript features (as seen in Figure 4). It
also provides support data for NodeJS and different JavaScript transpilers.
Data for these tables are collected with a test suite. [11]

22

Background

Figure 4. Example support data from ECMAScript compatibility tables page for Array.prototype.includes()

23

3. Case Study

This chapter focuses on the Iltalehti news website. The first section introduces the history of the Iltalehti tabloid newspaper and the Internet
version of Iltalehti. The second section gives an overview of the technology
behind the Iltalehti website. Then in the third section, the current transpilation setup for the website codebase is introduced and on the fourth
automated testing setup for this site. Lastly, the objectives for this work
are explained.

3.1

Iltalehti News Website

Iltalehti is a Finnish tabloid newspaper and an online service. Iltalehti
is owned by Alma Media Oyj and is part of the Alma Media Consumer
business unit. The newspaper is published six times a week, from Monday
to Saturday. In addition to newspapers, there are magazines, mainly
focusing on history or lifestyle. [18]
The web version of Iltalehti first appeared in 1995 with the name of
Iltalehti Online. At that time news was released only once a day. From
2005 onward news was published continuously and in 2006 Iltalehti Online
was renamed Iltalehti.fi and later to just Iltalehti. [18]
The main content of the Iltalehti site is news. Additionally, it contains a
weather forecast service, sports results, TV listings, and an electric version
of the Iltalehti newspaper. Iltalehti is also available as a mobile application
for both iOS and Android, which contains most of the same content as is
appearing on the site. Iltalehti site is responsive and scales from mobile
size to desktop size.
Today Iltalehti is one of the most popular sites in Finland with a reach of
2 796 119 visitors and 137 360 368 page views on week 26 of 2021. (FIAM
Media Site Toplist [12].)

24

Case Study

In 2020, Iltalehti website averaged 14.4 million page views per day
according to Google Analytics. Mobile and tablet usage accounts for 75% of
these pageviews. The users had on average 4.0 million sessions per day.

3.2

Technology Overview

Iltalehti’s website is built using the SPA model, where the client is a
JavaScript application running in a web browser, and view updates are
done by requesting new data from backend APIs and the page is updated
without page change occurring. This model moves a lot of logic into the
client portion of the website (that is running in a browser), and thus requirements for easier development in client code and required functionality
from browser APIs are higher compared to more traditional sites with multiple pages and more logic on the server-side. The website uses SSR to
achieve faster page load times.
The codebase for the website is programmed in JavaScript using features
from ES 2018 and earlier. Styles are written in Sass language, which
compiles to CSS. Major libraries include React for rendering, Redux for
state management and Moment for date and time handling. On the serverside Express.js is used to handle incoming HTTP requests.
The client application source code is split into multiple chunks to make
the initial page load lighter by loading only the code required by this specific page. New chunks are loaded dynamically when the user navigates
around the site, for example, when the user navigates to the page containing a weather forecast a “weather” chunk is loaded to the web browser.
This new chunk contains the functionality required for the weather forecast page. This way page loads are lighter (have less downloaded content),
and thus load faster.
Both Iltalehti website and mobile applications use the same backend
APIs to provide content. Different requirements for clients are handled
by customizing API responses with URL query parameters. The backend
APIs follow REST or GRAPHQL architecture and use JSON as a data
format.
The backend APIs providing news articles have the following technology
stack: Data storage of articles and related content is provided by PostgreSQL database and for search functionality, article text content is stored
on ElasticSearch. Images are stored on AWS S3 and go through a dynamic
scaling program Thumbor [37]. APIs connected to databases are written

25

Case Study

in Ruby programming language and follow REST architecture.
Our hosting provider is Amazon Web Services. Most applications are
hosted in the AWS Elastic Beanstalk service. It provides automatically
managed EC2 instances (AWS term for their virtualized servers) with load
balancers and deployment scripts for different programming languages and
web service runtimes. Data storage is done using managed services (such
as AWS RDS for PostgreSQL) that provide these services with minimal
maintenance work. Iltalehti is one of the most popular websites in Finland
and as such, it needs to handle a high rate of HTTP requests coming from
users. Fortunately, most requests are only fetching data and most data
is identical to all users. In this situation, caching is an effective way to
reduce the load on backend services. For caching HTTP responses we use
AWS Cloudfront CDN and Redis database.
Most source code repositories have automated deployment and testing
pipelines (CI and CD) that deliver source code changes to servers.

3.3

Current Transpilation Setup

The Iltalehti web application is built using Webpack [42]. Webpack supports multiple file types in addition to JavaScript with plugins (e.g., CSS,
JSON, and images, as seen in the Listing 12).
import styles from './styles.css';
import image from './image.jpg';

Listing 12. Webpack adds support for importing other than JavaScript files from
JavaScript. What actually happens in these imports is configurable in Webpack configuration. This way code can dynamically add styles to a page or get
an image URL from the imported image.

The Webpack build process is configurable with configuration files and
plugins. Transpilation is run in a Webpack plugin as part of the build
process. For JavaScript transpilation, Babel.js is used through babel-loader
(loader is Webpack’s term for a plugin that processes certain file types in
the build process). Styles are first compiled from Sass to plain CSS with
sass-loader and then processed with postcss-loader, that runs them through
autoprefixer and cssnano. Autoprefixer will transpile CSS to support older
versions of a browser and CSSnano will minify files for smaller file sizes.
Both Autoprefixes and CSSnano are plugins for PostCSS. Table 1 lays out
these stages. Browserslist is used to define a list of supported browsers for
both Babel and Autoprefixer.

26

Case Study

Webpack loader
transpilation
minification

JavaScript

CSS

babel-loader
Babel with preset-env
terser

sass-loader
autoprefixer
cssnano

Table 1. Stages of JavaScript and CSS build processes

For JavaScript, all code inside the repository is transpiled, but dependencies (in this case files inside node_modules) are excluded, as library
authors usually handle browser compatibility already. With preset-env
from Babel, source code is analyzed for all used language features and
polyfills for these are inserted automatically.
Because dependencies are not analyzed, these need manually defined
polyfill imports. (They are usually documented in these dependencies, e.g.,
React documents that it needs Map and Set polyfills).

3.3.1

Server-Side Rendering

SSR is used in the Iltalehti website on all pages. SSR allows caching
HTML files in our CDN for better first-page load times. However, this
requires that the content is not user-specific. User-specific content, such as
the name of logged in user, are excluded from server-side rendered pages,
and instead constructed in the web browser.
SSR requires running the application in a server using NodeJS and so it
adds a requirement for transpilation setup to support NodeJS as a runtime.
The version of NodeJS on the server is controllable, so the requirement is
not as hard as for web browser versions as the version can be upgraded
if needed. In our case, we do a separate build for the server-side version
of the application. This way it can be optimized for NodeJS, which needs
special polyfills for some functionalities found in browsers. For example,
Fetch API is not available on NodeJS and needs to be included as a library.

3.3.2

Two Bundles

For JavaScript files two different builds are done: one supporting more
“modern” browsers and another supporting “legacy” browsers. That makes
file sizes smaller for the majority of users as most users will be using the
modern bundle. Supporting all wanted browsers will make file sizes larger
because they need more polyfills for missing features and more language
syntax needs to be transpiled.

27

Case Study

This split is achieved by having two script tags on the page for every
file. “Modern” bundle targets browsers that support JavaScript modules,
“legacy” the rest. Listing 13 contains a snippet of HTML that demonstrates
how it is done with one JavaScript file.
<script nomodule="" src="/assets/client.legacy.js"></script>
<script type="module" src="/assets/client.js"></script>

Listing 13. Serving different files to browsers supporting JavaScript modules and to those
not supporting them using nomodule="" and type="module" attributes on
script tags.

Module support is a convenient cutoff for bundles, as browsers will
automatically detect, which script to load when both are inserted on a
page. Other cutoffs would need some logic to be run on the browsers before
downloading scripts, or on the server delivering scripts to detect browsers
from User-Agent header.
Some manual overrides are done on the modern bundle to drop polyfills,
as the automatic process will polyfill some features in browsers that support them if they have small bugs or some part of a feature is missing. But,
of course, this needs some validation that our code is not hitting these bugs
or using missing features. It is done to make bundles smaller.
The modern and legacy bundle split is done in addition to chunk splitting
for different pages or website functionality. All splitting is automated, so
releasing a new version of the website is not more cumbersome, but a bit
slower as multiple builds are done for a single release. This leads to twice
the amount of chunk files. Splitting to more bundles will cause a lower hit
rate on the CDN cache as not all users would use the same files. In reality,
it is negligible, as file updates are rare (at most a few times a day) and
cache TTL is infinite.
The legacy build uses a list of browser versions defined in the code-base.
The modern build is done with a simple Browserslist query that defines all
browsers that support JavaScript modules. As CSS can not use the module
support technique that JavaScript uses, all CSS is compiled to target the
legacy browsers list.
Currently, the current list of browsers is outdated and contains versions that are not actually supported, as it has not been updated recently.
Revising the list can yield smaller target file sizes, as only needed code
transformations will be done.

28

Case Study

3.4

Current Automated End-to-End Tests

The current end-to-end (e2e) testing setup uses Puppeteer [33] library for
browser automation with jest-puppeteer to connect puppeteer to test runner
Jest. The Puppeteer library uses Chrome’s DevTools Protocol to control
the browser and so it is specific to Chrome. It is not itself a testing library
and is just designed to programmatically control Chrome. That is why an
additional library (jest-puppeteer) is needed for writing tests and run them.
Unit tests in the codebase use Jest testing framework.
These tests are run against a locally running copy of the website and they
are run automatically on every git pull request on a CI service to ensure
that every change to codebase passes these tests. Additionally, a developer
can run them on their computer to test changes before submitting a pull
request.
These tests are run against real APIs. Most functionality on the website
is read-only and currently, no test does any change that would modify
resources on the backend, which would mean issuing POST or PATCH
requests. This way these tests can be run even against production APIs.
Most tests look like the example test in the Listing 14. The format is
simple: navigate to a page to be tested and then assert that it contains
certain elements.
describe('Thing to test', () => {
it('Should find correct elements on /url/to/test', async () => {
await page.goto(`${testURL}/url/to/test`);
await expect(page).toMatchElement('.element-on-page', { text: 'Some text' });
// .. more assertions.
});
});

Listing 14. Example about how tests look like.

Some issues have been encountered with the current testing setup.
Firstly, tests can only be run on Chrome and Chromium (and experimentally on Firefox) and not on other browsers. Instead, manual testing
is needed to ensure that changes work on other browsers. Secondly, puppeteer dependency installs a version of Chromium with itself, as it requires
a specific version of Chromium to ensure API compatibility. This leads to a
large project deploy archive which triggers the AWS Elastic Beanstalk file
size limit.

29

4. Implementation

This chapter focuses on the implementation of work objectives as outlined
in the first chapter. It contains three parts. The first is an analysis of
browsers used to visit Iltalehti. The second is improvements made to the
website transpilation setup. The third is improvements made to testing in
different browsers.

4.1

Analysis of Browser Versions

Usage of different browser versions in the Iltalehti website is needed
for refining transpilation setup and automated testing. This section will
explain how this usage data is gathered and present conclusions from this
data to support transpilation and testing changes.

4.1.1

Data Sources

Data sources are Google Analytics and AWS CloudFront access statistics
of the Iltalehti website. Additionally, global browser usage data included
with the Browserslist tool is used. This data comes from StatCounter
GlobalStats and it is used by default in queries if nothing else is specified.
[10] [8]
It should be noted that Google Analytics data does not contain exactly
all users visiting the Iltalehti website, as the Google Analytics tracking
script is enabled only if the user accepts its usage in the consent popup.
The user is presented with a consent popup when visiting the website first
time with a new browser. Some users block Google Analytics script with
browser extensions, and on some browsers, this blocking is built in the
browser itself. In conclusion, this means that this data does not cover 100%
of users. This is not a problem in AWS Cloudfront statistics because they
are gathered server-side from file access statistics. In our measurements,

30

Implementation

about 3% of users do not give consent in the popup.

4.1.2

Browserslists Custom Usage Data

Browserslist allows using your own custom usage data in queries as explained in Section 2.5. This data needs to be provided in its own file in
a certain format. Browserslist provides a tool for converting page views
in a CSV file from Google Analytics to this Browserlist’s format. This
conversion script is called browserslist-ga-export. [8]
The data outputted by conversion tool can be used in queries in format
> 2\% in my stats where in my stats refers to custom data and so in that

query Browserslist would select browser version, which has more than
2% of page views. The conversion tool takes CSV from Google Analytics
as input and outputs JSON file, which contains key-value pairs for each
browser version and its usage percentage.
This custom usage data was tested by taking instructed custom report
from Google Analytics of Iltalehti. A 30-day interval was selected (from
2020-10-07 to 2020-11-05). This report did contain more than 5000 rows,
so it had to be generated as an unsampled report in Google Analytics,
deviating from instructions. This report is a CSV file that was given as
input for the conversion tool provided by browserslist-ga-export.

Figure 5. Five browsers with most
pageviews according to Google
Analytics.

Figure 6. Seven browsers with highest usage percentage from
browserslist-ga-export.

Unfortunately, this conversion tool leaves a portion of browsers unclassified. For example, straight from Google Analytics data in Figure 5
Samsung Internet browser is third in usage, but in outputted statistics
file, it has usage of 0%. Figure 6 shows seven most used browsers from
browserslist-ga-export outputted data.
Additionally, coverage percentage is significantly lower compared to

31

Implementation

global usage data and usage data from Finland in the same queries in
Listing 5 and in Listing 2, which also indicates that the data is not correct.
If more browsers were classified, this data could be used on Browserslist
query in Italehti website. This way only custom data needed to periodically be updated and targeted browsers would update automatically. Now,
this custom usage data can be used to evaluate other queries, but some
uncertainty must be accounted for in the results.

4.1.3

Legacy Browser Usage

We can estimate the share of users using the legacy bundle from web
server file access statistics. The legacy bundle is JavaScript files targeted at browsers not supporting ES modules. In this case, we are using
www.iltalehti.fi AWS Cloudfront file access statistics. Taking a sample by
looking at file access from a day 2021-05-04 and comparing request count
to JavaScript files with "legacy" in their name and those with not. This
results in around 2.4% share of legacy requests in total requests.
This data is not exactly accurate because some browsers using modern
bundles will also download legacy bundles, which counts in file access
statistics. ([6] note about Edge versions 15-18). But it works as a rough
estimate.
browserslist --coverage '> 0\% and not supports es6-module'
browserslist --coverage '> 0\% in FI and not supports es6-module'
browserslist --coverage '> 0\% in my stats and not supports es6-module'

Listing 15. Browserslist queries to get legacy browser usage percentage against global,
from Finland and our statistics.

Another way to estimates legacy browser usage is by using browserslists
with queries in Listing 15. We compare the same query against three
statistics: global, from Finland (majority of users in Iltalehti are from
Finland), and our custom statistics. Results for usage, which is the same
as Browserslists reported coverage, are in Table 2. Usage from custom
statistics is low, probably because of problems in statistics parsing, and it
is excluded. In conclusion estimate of usage is between 1.5% to 5.1%.
In the light of these numbers, it can be asked if the legacy build is useful.
The legacy build serves only a small portion of users, but with our usage
numbers, the absolute value of users is still high. As stated in Section
3.1, Iltalehti website averaged 14.4 million page views per day, from which
only 1% is still 144 000 page views, which as an absolute value is still
considerable. The legacy build was decided to be kept.

Implementation

4.1.4

Google Analytics Page View Analysis

As the Browserslist custom usage statistics were not accurate, a further
analysis is needed to be done to support the decision of which browser
versions to support. The same page view data from Google Analytics, which
was used as input to Browserslist, was used. This Google Analytics report
contains browser name and version, OS name and version, device category
(mobile, tablet, or desktop), and page view count.
Some cleanup was done on this data. The Safari browser version is
not reported on Safari iOS in-app page views, so it was copied from the
operating system version, as the Safari version is the same as the iOS
version. Safari in-app pageviews were renamed to just Safari as it should
be the same browser. After cleanup, the sum of page views without browser
version is 0.015%, which is small enough that it should not affect conclusions. Before cleanup sum of page views without browser version was
significantly higher.
The target is to find a minimum version for each browser in pageviews,
that has usage over some cutoff percentage. This is needed to specify what
are the minimum browser versions that we need to support and can be
used as a basis for updated Browserslist query and in which versions to
run automated integration testing.
Only the major version of the browser is taken into account. This is
done because major versions should contain larger feature changes and
make compared version groups larger. This does not make all browsers
exactly equal in comparisons, as it can give browsers making releases less
frequently more users in versions, and this way they can have more weight
in this method.
Usage cutoff percentage starting point was decided to be 0.5%, as it is
the same as in Browserslist defaults query, which is defined as in Listing
16). The defaults query contains other conditions as well.
Table 3 shows minimum major browser versions with usage over 0.3%

Coverage of minimum browser versions in Table 3 can be computed from
same page view data. Coverage tells the percentage of page views that
have the same or higher browser version. If a browser does not appear in
Listing it is counted as 0.
Cutoff of 0.3% and lower leads to old versions that need more work to
support than just automated transpilation. Safari 10.1 does not support
our module and nomodule split as it does not support nomodule attribute.
[10] It supports ES modules, but it will download both scripts and execute
both of them, which will lead to errors on the page. Currently, Safari 10.1
and lower do not work correctly on the Iltalehti website, some pages are
readable because SSR will render them and styles are working in them,
but more interactive parts of the website (e.g., weather forecast page) does
not work at all.
Cutoff of 0.3% was selected, with coverage of 95.7%, but the Safari version
has to be raised to 11. Higher coverage percentage would have been great,
but achieving that would need changes to the codebase.

Table 5. Coverage for 3 compared browserlist queries. The first (Global) is against browserslist global usage data. The second (Custom) is from usage data from Iltalehti
Google Analytics using browserslist custom usage feature. And the last is our
own Google Analytics based usage statistics.

Table 5 shows a comparison of reported query coverage. It tells how
many users the query will cover. Browserslist values are produced with
--coverage option in the Browserslist tool. Google Analytics-based numbers

are calculated from page view data by filtering it with browser major
version condition. This is why the defaults query has no data, as it doesn’t
rely on certain browser versions that we could use for filtering.
This reported percentage is not exactly on how many percentages of
users the page is working, because it just tells if Browserslist’s output,
which is just a long list of browsers and versions, will contain browsers and
versions in usage statistics. Page can still work even if a certain browser
is not listed. Many browsers are based on Chromium (Opera, new Edge,
Samsung Browser) [7] and so specifying Chrome as a supported browser
should add support for these. This explains low coverage for the current
query, as it is missing some browsers, but it does not mean that the page
is not working on them.
Tables 6 and 7 contain comparisons of file sizes when adjusting the
Browserslist query. They contain the three compared queries and file size
reduction percentage for the seven largest files and for the sum of all files.
Compared files are the end result of the Webpack build process and these
files would be served to client browsers in production.
Reductions in file sizes are not major, around 1%, and the new query
seems to be better with a reduction of 1.4%.
Curiously, file size changes are very similar in size when comparing modern and legacy file sizes, as this query should affect only legacy bundles
and CSS. The modern bundle is done with a query that targets browsers

with ES modules support. Chunks containing only libraries, e.g. vendors client.chunk.js that is a chunk that contains all common libraries

change comes from CSS, which is inside JavaScript files and is transpiled
with the same query for both builds. When excluding CSS from these
builds the size differences change as seen in Tables 8 and 9.
CSS is transpiled with the same configuration for legacy and modern
builds because of SSR. The HTML page returned from SSR contains styles
for this page and this page is cached in Cloudfront, so it must support all
browsers. It could be possible to compile CSS with legacy config for serverside build for NodeJS and with modern and legacy config for respective
builds.
Change difference between a current and new query in JavaScript size is
minimal, only 0.15% in legacy build and 0% on modern.

4.3

Automated Tests on Multiple Browsers

The objective of these changes to tests is to ensure that website will work
on multiple browsers. Already existing testing setup was used as a base
and it was changed to run on multiple browsers. Results from browser
analysis were used to determine on which browser version tests are run.
Testing will check that transpilation is working and additionally raise
testing coverage on other changes to the code base that affect website
support on different browsers.
The following two sections describe the selected testing library and
browser testing service. The selection process of the testing library is
not the focus of this work, this is just one possible solution.

4.3.1

Browser Testing Service

Testing on multiple browsers requires that these browsers are available
somewhere. An external service called Browserstack is used for this

38

Implementation

purpose. It provides a range of browsers and mobile devices for automated
and manual testing. [5]
Browserstack offers "live" testing for manually testing websites on different browsers, which can be used to, e.g., reproduce bugs and to check
that styles work correctly. For automated testing, Browserstack offers integration with multiple e2e testing frameworks. Video playback is available
from executed automated tests. [5]
Tests using Browserstack can be run on CI pipeline or locally on the
developer’s computer. The actual browser runs in BrowserStack’s services
and not on the computer that is running these tests. Authentication is
done by username and password in environment variables. [5]

4.3.2

New Testing Library

Testcafe is an end-to-end testing library for web testing, that was selected
as a replacement library.
Testcafe supports cross-browser testing, meaning that tests can be run
on multiple different browsers. It is not based on WebDriver protocol and
Selenium and instead, it uses its own JavaScript library and proxy for
running tests. [36]
It also provides automated waiting, as no waiting commands are needed
in testing code. This is done with a technique that Testcafe calls Smart
Assertation Query. Normally, waiting commands are needed when, e.g.,
web page updates page asynchronously and tests have to wait for page
update before it can assert what its content is. Testcafe’s Smart Assertation
Query mechanism work by retrying assertation multiple times until it
passes or a timeout is reached. [36]
Additionally, Testcafe automatically detects any JavaScript errors on the
page under tests and fails the test. This is a convenient way to detect if
the transpilation setup produces JavaScript that, e.g., causes syntax error
in the browser. [36]
Testcafe was selected because it is used by other projects in Alma Media and it provided cross-browser testing, which is important for testing
support in multiple browsers, which is our goal. Support for Browserstack
integration was also needed and Testcafe does support this.

39

Implementation

4.3.3

Changes to Tests

Changes to end-to-end tests were started by converting all tests to use
Testcafe instead of Puppeteer. This was a mostly straightforward operation,
and Listing 19 shows that a typical Testcafe test is not that different from
previous tests.
import { Selector } from 'testcafe';
import { testUrl, requestHooks } from '../../../tests/integrationHelpers';
fixture`Thing to test`.requestHooks(requestHooks);
test('Should find correct elements on /url/to/test', async (t) => {
await t.navigateTo(`${testUrl}/url/to/test`);
await t.expect(Selector('.element-on-page').textContent).contains('Some text');
// ... more assertions
});

Listing 19. Example tests using Testcafe.

At first, the test suite was only run locally against Chrome to make
developing easier. Testcafe supports running device emulation in Chrome,
which makes the viewport smaller. One target with device emulation was
added to the test suite (chrome:emulation:device=iphone X) to ensure that
tests work on smaller screens. In Browserstack tests, there will be mobile
devices, and this way we could prepare for smaller screens. This device
emulation does not replace testing on the actual browser and device, as e.g.
JavaScript is still executed on Chrome JS engine and not on Safari when
emulating iPhone.
Three different options to run tests were created. Two of them to run
tests locally on Chrome, one in a headless mode where the browser window
is hidden, and one where it is visible. The third option is running tests
in Browserstack. Locally run versions are used when developing tests
and when a developer wants to test against changes made locally. The
Browserstack version is run on the CI environment.
To support testing mobile devices with smaller screens, some tests needed
changes. For example, many pages have a side column on the right of the
page on desktop size screens, but on mobile sizes, it is moved to the end
of the page. This side column is lazy-loaded and the user must scroll to it
before it is loaded. This means that in tests we need to scroll to the bottom
of the page and then to the side column element before it can be asserted
that it appears on the page.
Testcafe’s JavaScript error detection did not work well with advertise-

40

Implementation

ments as they can introduce errors in the page that are unrelated to the
page under test. To solve this advertisements were disabled in tests by
using Testcafe’s request mocking capabilities. However, this error detection
was found to be a useful way to find bugs on the website.
The selection of tested browser versions was done in a similar way as
for the new Browserlist query. Additionally, we needed to examine what
browsers are available on Browserstack. The number of tested browsers
should also be kept low as we have a maximum limit of 5 parallel browsers
on Browserstack. A higher number than 5 could be used, but it would
double the time taken by tests, as some tests have to wait until more
capacity is available.
We are only testing on the lowest major version of browsers. There can
be bugs between the versions, but testing all of these versions takes too
much time and resources. The tested browsers were taken from Table 3 in
a similar way as the browserslist configuration.
Browser

Chromium version

Samsung Internet 9.0
Opera 60
Edge 79

Chromium 67
Chromium 73
Chromium 79

Table 10. Chromium version for Chromium-based browsers. For Edge oldest Chromiumbased version is used. [16] [17] [25]

To keep the number of tested browsers low, as there are limitations for
the number of parallel tests, Chromium-based browsers were replaced
with Chrome with the lowest corresponding version number in these
browsers. Table 10 shows corresponding Chromium versions for each
replaced browser. Additionally, Samsung Internet is not available on
Browserstack in a way that allows selecting a specific version number.
Browsers, which are not Chromium-based and are instead independent
implementations (e.g., Chrome, Edge (older versions), Firefox, Safari, Internet Explorer), are more important to tests as they should have more
differences in their support for features.
The majority of page views comes from mobile devices in Iltalehti, as seen
in Figure 7. So, testing on mobile devices is important. Not so much in
transpilation perspective, as the browser is the same on desktop and mobile
on Android and iOS, the two most popular mobile operating systems.
The Listing 20 shows the selected browser and their versions in a format
that Browserstack uses to define them. The list from Table 18 was reduced
to just 4 items for the following reasons. The concurrent testing limit

Listing 20. Configured Browserstack browsers based on Table 18.

on browserstack is 5 browsers, under which a number of tested browsers
wanted to be kept. The Browserstack integration of Testcafe does not
support out-of-box queuing these tests if they go over the limit. Chrome
and Chromium-based browser were reduced to a single version of Chrome,
in an assumption that they will behave the same. IE 11 was dropped from
this list as it was found that some tests did not pass on it, and it would
have been a lot of work to add support for IE11. However, most pages of
Iltalehti still work in IE11, so it was still kept in the new browserslist
query.

Table 11. Test suite duration compared.

Table 11 shows test suite durations from before and after changes. Duration is measured locally on the same laptop and on the CI run. Some
differences can come from different timings from API calls to external
systems and the load on the computer where tests are run, but they should
be minor. The duration is an average of four measurements. CI measures
running the whole test suite, including unit tests. Measures are taken
from an average of 4 runs.
The following errors or bugs were found in tests:

42

Implementation

• Safari 10.1 missing support for nomodul attribute in script tags leads to
all pages not working correctly.

• IE11 not working on multiple pages. Most of them do contain embedded
content, which source code is outside of the Iltalehti website repository,
so it is not under the same transpilation setup.

These were found when running the test suite on different browsers. It
shows that at least in these cases testing did find pages not working on
certain browsers. Some of these were known before, but now they can
easily be discovered by just running the test suite.

43

5. Discussion

In this chapter, results of this thesis are discussed. First, transpilation
setup changes are analyzed, then testing changes and lastly alternatives
to transpilation are compared.

5.1

5.1.1

Refining Transpilation Setup

RQ1: What is the coverage of the current transpilation
setup in browsers used to visit the Iltalehti website and
can a higher coverage percentage be achieved?

The current browser coverage percentage was 89% and the new is 96%,
so a higher coverage percentage was achieved. But this does not mean
that in reality, the website supports more browsers, just that the new
listing contains more browsers. A fully accurate picture of the previous
browser support level would require analyzing what is supported outside
the listing.
These numbers come from Table 5 and refer to my own analysis using data from Google Analytics. The coverage percentage that is got
from Browserslist is not very meaningful, as it requires that all different
browsers are listed, even if, for example, they are just different Chromiumbased browsers. Additionally, the coverage percentage is very low (56%),
which doesn’t seem realistic. A higher coverage percentage can be achieved,
but not without other changes to the code-base, not just by adjusting targeted browsers.
About data gathering. The first tried solution to analyze browser access
statistics, browserslist-ga-export, was not a satisfactory solution, as it left
data unclassified. A manual analysis of page views was done to determine
browser versions usage statistics. This solution needs manual updating

44

Discussion

of browser versions, but it is clear when support for a browser is done
because the query must be changed. This might affect what manually
added polyfills are needed.
The following issues should be considered about the accuracy of these
results. When evaluating browser access statistics, it is possible that
people for which the page is not working are not visiting the website, and
thus they don’t show up in the statistics. And additionally, the web page
can be working well enough on a certain browser, even if that browser is
not covered by our query. For example, a page can be visually complete
due to SSR even when JavaScript code is not working on the page. And a
user can still use most web pages.

5.1.2

RQ2: How much does adjusting targeted browsers affect
file sizes?

File sizes were smaller after changes, but these changes were minimal
(around -1.6%). Most changes did come from CSS changes. CSS is a smaller
portion of the total sum of file sizes than JavaScript, so it was unexpected
that it created more file size savings. The reason is that CSS does not use
the legacy and modern split that JavaScript uses, which already does keep
file sizes down. Instead, all outputted CSS targets the legacy browsers set.

5.2

5.2.1

Automated Tests on Multiple Browsers

RQ3: Can browser support be tested with end-to-end tests
and what are the advantages and disadvantages of testing
on multiple browsers?

Automated testing can be certainly used, but it comes with some downsides.
JavaScript error detection seems to be a good way to detect browser support
and it makes finding the cause easy. SSR in the Iltalehti website makes
finding errors a bit harder, as the page will display most of the content
even if JavaScript is not working on it. For validating CSS this automated
testing solution does nothing, and it will still need manual testing.
The advantages of automated testing on multiple browsers are less
manual testing and higher confidence of support in different browsers.
Disadvantages are slower testing at least in technologies used in this case
study and fewer testing frameworks are available that support multiple

45

Discussion

browsers.
Some bugs relating to browser support were found and it shows that this
can be used to detect those. Of course, testing will not show that bugs are
nonexistent.
Tests are significantly slower when run on Testcafe, they take 155%
longer when run locally on 857% longer on CI. The slowdown comes from
the testing library change and on CI running on multiple browsers brings
additional slowness. Previously, tests were run on a browser installed on
the CI virtual machine, now they are run on Browserstack, where starting
a test takes more time.
Subjectively it seems that this testing setup is more error-prone and even
if some tests were to pass on some browsers, it could fail on others due
to timing issues. Also, some connectivity issues with Browserstack were
encountered, which made tests fail.

5.3

Advantages and Disadvantages of Transpiling

There are other possibilities than transpiling JS and CSS for achieving
support for multiple browsers in a website.
One obvious choice is to develop the website for the lowest supported
browser. In this case, source code for the website is not transpiled and
instead served to a web browser as is. Positives for this approach are a
simpler build process, as transpilation is not needed, and debugging is
easier as source code is similar to executed code. Negatives are developer
ergonomics, as developers need to use only older language features, and
testing might be needed to ensure that accidentally unsupported features
are not used. Some limitedly available browser APIs can be replaced with
libraries, like the Fetch API.
Another option is just not supporting older browsers. It might be feasible
depending on the audience, for example, on internal websites for a company
that is accessed only on company computers that have a certain known
browser installed. Or alternatively, some web applications whose main
function needs some new feature in browsers to function so it would be
unnecessary to try to get other parts of the application to work in other
browsers. Nearly all websites need some cutoff of what browsers they can
support and so this option is used with other choices.
So, in conclusion, the advantages are that developers can use the newest
language features and APIs. And disadvantages are the larger file size due

46

Discussion

to added polyfills and verbose transpilation output, as seen in our results
legacy build is larger than modern build.

47

6. Conclusions

This work was focused on how transpilation setup in the Iltalehti website
could be made better. First, it focused on how transpilation works and
how it is used in web development to support more browsers and allow
developers to use the latest language versions. Then, how transpilation
and polyfills are used in the Iltalehti website. This work showed how
browser usage data can be used to adjust what browsers are targeted and
what advantages it can bring. It also showed that testing can be used
to validate browser support, which can be used to show that the wanted
browser support level is achieved.
The browser support was good before these changes and no major increase
happened from my changes. However, a more accurate view of which
browsers are used and how much of them the website does support was
acquired. It can be a good idea to adjust the list of targeted browsers from
time to time as it will reduce files sizes.
Even when the browser is listed in targeted browsers, the website may
well not work and automated testing can be used to reveal that. Oppositely
the page can very well work on a certain browser even if it is not listed in
supported browsers. However, automated testing on multiple browsers did
come with its downsides.
